title: "The tests"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
if (!file.exists("data/wss_clean.rds")) source("R/01_recode.R")
```

A test is how you make a verification **permanent**. You will check a recode once by
hand; you will not check it again in six weeks when somebody — you, a collaborator, an
agent — "improves" it. `testthat` turns the check into something that fails on its own.

## What `testthat` is

R's unit-testing package. A test file is ordinary R code that **asserts** rather than
prints: it states what must be true and fails loudly when it is not. Files live in
`tests/testthat/` and are named `test-*.R`.

```r
test_that("what must be true", {
  expect_true(...)
})
```

The string is the failure message, so write it as a claim.

| Expectation | Asserts |
|---|---|
| `expect_equal(x, y)` | equal within numerical tolerance |
| `expect_identical(x, y)` | exactly identical |
| `expect_true(x)` | all of `x` is `TRUE` |
| `expect_setequal(x, y)` | same values, any order |
| `expect_length(x, n)` | length is `n` |
| `expect_error(f())` | it *does* fail |
| `expect_no_warning(f())` | it runs clean |
| `skip("reason")` | not applicable in this environment |

## Two kinds of test

The suite is split by what each test needs in order to run, because that is what
determines how fast it is and how precisely it points at a failure.

| | Unit | Integration |
|---|---|---|
| Files | `test-unit-*.R` | `test-integration-*.R` |
| What it tests | one function | the pieces working together |
| Input | synthetic, written in the test | the real CSV, the built `.rds`, the app |
| Fails when | the function's logic is wrong | the wiring is wrong |
| Runs in | milliseconds | seconds |

A unit test for `bin_age()` tells you the breaks moved. An integration test on
`data/wss_clean.rds` tells you *something* upstream changed. You want both: the first
is precise, the second is what actually catches the agent that edited the recode and
broke the app.

::: {.note}
[Unit tests need units]{.note-head}
A 200-line script has nothing to unit-test. The reason `R/functions.R` exists — pure
helpers taking data in and returning data out, no reading, no writing — is that it
makes the recode's logic testable without the survey file at all. Extracting the
functions came first; the tests came second.
:::

### Unit: the recode helpers

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| class-output: sourceCode
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/test-unit-recode.R"), sep = "\n")
```

Every input here is written out in the test. Nothing on disk can make these pass or
fail, so when one goes red the fault is in the function and nowhere else.

### Unit: the estimator

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| class-output: sourceCode
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/test-unit-estimates.R"), sep = "\n")
```

A five-row frame whose weighted mean you can do in your head is worth more than a
thousand real rows whose answer you would have to trust.

### Integration: the pipeline

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| class-output: sourceCode
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/test-integration-pipeline.R"), sep = "\n")
```

Four properties worth asserting about any recode, all of them here: the **row count**
is unchanged, derived scales are **in range**, categorical variables take only
**documented** values, and the **analysis N** is what you think it is.

### Integration: the app

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| class-output: sourceCode
cat(readLines("tests/testthat/test-integration-app.R"), sep = "\n")
```

`shiny::testServer()` runs the server function without a browser: set inputs, read the
reactives. It caught a real bug while this chapter was being written — the server was
declared `function(input, output)`, and `testServer()` requires `session` as well.

## Running them

```{r}
#| label: run-tests
testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat", reporter = "progress")
```

From the shell, which is what you would put in CI:

```bash
Rscript -e 'testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")'
```

## What a failure looks like

Change a recode and the claim goes red. Here the assertion is deliberately wrong:

```{r}
#| label: demo-failure
#| error: true
library(testthat)
wss <- readRDS("data/wss_clean.rds")

test_that("trump_vote is coded for every respondent", {
  expect_equal(sum(!is.na(wss$trump_vote)), nrow(wss))
})
```

That is the useful output: the claim, the expected value, the actual value. A silent
recode error produces a number; a test produces this.

## Tests worth adding

- One per derived variable, asserting range and allowed values.
- One asserting `nrow()` after the recode — the cheapest guard against a join that
  multiplied rows.
- One asserting the **analysis N**, so a change in missingness cannot pass unnoticed.
- `expect_error()` on the input guard: if someone hands the recode a file without
  `auth1:auth4`, it should fail rather than produce `NaN`.

::: {.note}
[A good use of an agent]{.note-head}
*"Read `R/01_recode.R` and write a `testthat` test for every derived variable: range,
allowed values, and row count. Do not change the recode."*

Then read the tests. They are far easier to check than the recode they protect, and
reading them is how you find out whether the agent understood the codebook or guessed.
:::
